statement: A rectangle has an area of 36 and sides that are whole numbers. Which of these could NOT be its perimeter?

choices.misconception: I ruled out the square 6 by 6, forgetting that a square is a rectangle.
I did not think to try 4 by 9, so I judged this perimeter impossible.
I missed the 3 by 12 rectangle when listing the factor pairs.
I stopped listing factor pairs before reaching 2 by 18.

hints: Whole-number sides with area 36 means the sides are a factor pair of 36. List all the pairs, work out each perimeter, and see which offered value never appears.
The pairs are 1 and 36, 2 and 18, 3 and 12, 4 and 9, 6 and 6, giving perimeters 74, 40, 30, 26 and 24. There is no 28.

solutions.reliable: Whole-number sides multiplying to 36 must be a factor pair. The pairs are 1 x 36, 2 x 18, 3 x 12, 4 x 9 and 6 x 6, giving perimeters of 74, 40, 30, 26 and 24. Every offered value appears except 28, so 28 is impossible. The transferable idea: bounding and listing the possibilities rules choices out far faster than trying to construct the awkward one.
solutions.elegant: A perimeter of 28 needs sides adding to 14 and multiplying to 36, and no pair of whole numbers does both.

whyOnTest: Ruling choices out by what is possible is a different skill from computing an answer, and it is the one a could-not question demands.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
